lesson.title: Choosing a Legal Home for a Business: Proprietorship to Corporation
lesson.summary: Businesses can be set up in several legal forms, and each form splits control, personal risk, taxes, fundraising ability and lifespan differently. The exam expects you to match a business situation to the form that fits it best.

sections.heading: The core trade-offs
sections.body_markdown:
Every legal form answers the same five questions:

1. **Who is on the hook for the business's debts?** (liability)
2. **Who pays tax on the profits, and how many times?**
3. **How easy is it to bring in outside money?**
4. **Does the business survive if an owner leaves or dies?**
5. **Who makes decisions?**

Think of the legal form as the wrapper around the business. A thin wrapper (a sole proprietorship) is cheap and simple but offers no protection. A thick wrapper (a corporation) protects the owners and attracts investors but costs more to set up and run.

sections.heading: Sole proprietorships and general partnerships
sections.body_markdown:
A **sole proprietorship** is an unincorporated business owned by one person. It is cheap and quick to start, lightly regulated and fully controlled by the owner. Profits are reported on the owner's personal tax return, so they are taxed once.

The drawbacks:
- The owner has **unlimited liability**. Creditors can reach personal assets, so the owner can lose more than was invested.
- The business is tied to the owner's life.
- Funding is limited to the owner's own resources and borrowing ability.

A **general partnership** has two or more owners. It adds skills and capital, and income is allocated to the partners and taxed on their personal returns, so the partnership itself pays no income tax. But *each* general partner is exposed to unlimited liability, **including for a partner's mistakes**. Sharing decisions can also cause conflict.

A **limited partnership** has at least one general partner, who runs the business and bears unlimited liability. It also has limited partners, who are passive investors whose loss is capped at what they contributed.

sections.heading: Corporations and double taxation
sections.body_markdown:
A **corporation** is a legal entity separate from its owners (shareholders). It can sign contracts, own property, sue and be sued, and be taxed.

Advantages:
- **Limited liability**: shareholders can lose at most what they invested.
- **Unlimited life**: the entity outlives any shareholder.
- **Easy transfer of shares**, which makes the stock more liquid and makes it easier to raise large amounts of capital.

The main disadvantage is **double taxation**. Profits are taxed at the corporate level. When the after-tax profit is paid out as dividends, the shareholder is taxed again on the personal return.

Because limited liability lowers investors' risk and share transfer is easy, most large businesses end up as corporations. Many firms start as proprietorships or partnerships and convert as they grow.

Some jurisdictions let small corporations elect special tax treatment so that profit is taxed only at the owner level. The US "S corporation" is an example, and it is limited to a small number of shareholders. The large, standard corporation is the "C corporation".

sections.heading: Hybrids: LLCs and LLPs
sections.body_markdown:
Hybrid forms try to keep the best of both worlds. A **limited liability company (LLC)** gives its owners (members) liability protection like a corporation, but its profits typically pass through to the members' personal tax returns, as in a partnership. This avoids double taxation. Votes in an LLC generally follow ownership interest.

A **limited liability partnership (LLP)** is similar. It is common for professional firms such as law, accounting and architecture practices, and it protects partners from the negligence of other partners.

The rules and degree of protection vary by jurisdiction, and these forms are legally complex. Large companies that want to raise substantial outside capital still tend to favour the corporate form.

**Quick comparison**

| Form | Owner liability | Tax on profits | Raising capital |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sole proprietorship | Unlimited | Once, at owner | Hard |
| General partnership | Unlimited (shared) | Once, at partners | Somewhat easier |
| Limited partnership | Unlimited for general partner; limited for limited partners | Once, at partners | Better |
| LLC / LLP | Limited (strength varies) | Usually once (pass-through) | Moderate |
| Corporation | Limited | Twice if dividends paid | Easiest |

worked_example.problem: A business earns $100,000 before any income tax this year. Compare what the owner keeps if it is (a) a corporation that pays all its after-tax profit as a dividend, with a 25% corporate tax rate and a 20% personal tax rate on dividends, versus (b) a partnership taxed on the owner's personal return at 30%. Assume the owner holds 100% of the business in each case and ignore all other taxes.
steps: No calculator keystrokes are needed; this is simple percentage arithmetic.
Corporation, first layer of tax: $100,000 × 25% = $25,000, leaving $75,000 after corporate tax.
Corporation, the $75,000 is paid out as a dividend. Second layer of tax: $75,000 × 20% = $15,000.
Partnership: profit passes straight through to the owner's return. Tax = $100,000 × 30% = $30,000, so the owner keeps $70,000.
Difference: $70,000 − $60,000 = $10,000 more is lost to tax under the corporate structure in this example.
worked_example.answer: The owner keeps $60,000 under the corporation and $70,000 under the partnership, so double taxation costs $10,000 more here.

formulas.name: After-tax cash to owner when all profit is paid as a dividend (double taxation)
formulas.where: E = pre-tax business earnings; t_c = corporate income tax rate; t_d = personal tax rate on dividends; Net = cash kept by the shareholder.

formulas.name: After-tax cash to owner under pass-through taxation
formulas.where: E = pre-tax business earnings; t_p = owner's personal tax rate on business income; Net = cash kept by the owner.

exam_traps: Assuming every partner in a general partnership is only liable for their own actions. In fact each general partner can be liable for all the partnership's debts, including those caused by another partner.
Forgetting that limited partners must stay passive. The general partner runs the business and carries unlimited liability.
Believing corporate taxation is always worse. Double taxation only applies to profit that is distributed as dividends, and pass-through forms trade tax savings for weaker fundraising ability.
Treating LLCs as having the same liability protection and tax treatment everywhere. They are hybrids: limited liability like a corporation, usually pass-through tax like a partnership.
Mixing up liability and control: limited liability does not mean limited decision rights, and a sole proprietor has full control but also full personal risk.

mcqs.stem: Which business form exposes its owner to unlimited personal liability and taxes business profit only once, on the owner's personal return?

options.text: Sole proprietorship
options.explanation: Correct. The owner and business are the same legal person, so creditors can reach personal assets, and profit is reported only on the owner's own return.

options.text: Corporation paying dividends
options.explanation: Corporate profit is taxed at the corporate level and again on dividends, and shareholders have limited liability. This fails both tests.

options.text: Limited liability company
options.explanation: An LLC usually has pass-through tax, but its members have limited liability, so this fails the liability test.

mcqs.stem: In a limited partnership, which statement about the limited partners is correct?

options.text: They run daily operations and carry unlimited liability for the debts.
options.explanation: This describes the general partner, not a limited partner. It confuses the two partner types.

options.text: They share unlimited liability equally with the general partner.
options.explanation: Unlimited liability belongs to the general partner. Limited partners are not exposed to all the debts.

options.text: They are passive and can lose only the amount they contributed.
options.explanation: Correct. Limited partners have limited involvement in the business and their loss is capped at their investment.

mcqs.stem: A general partnership goes bankrupt because one partner mismanaged the business. The firm's assets do not cover its debts. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Creditors can pursue the other general partners' personal assets for the unpaid debts.
options.explanation: Correct. General partners have unlimited liability, including for the partnership's debts caused by another partner's actions.

options.text: Only the partner who mismanaged the business can be pursued by creditors.
options.explanation: This wrongly assumes liability follows fault. In a general partnership each partner can be liable for the firm's debts.

options.text: Each partner can lose only the amount originally invested in the firm.
options.explanation: This describes limited liability, as in a corporation or for limited partners. It does not apply to general partners.

mcqs.stem: Which feature best explains why most large businesses are organized as corporations rather than as partnerships?

options.text: Corporate profits are never taxed, which leaves more cash for expansion.
options.explanation: Corporate earnings are taxed, and dividends can be taxed again. This confuses corporations with pass-through entities.

options.text: Shareholders' liability is limited and shares transfer easily, which helps raise capital.
options.explanation: Correct. Limited liability lowers investor risk, and easily transferable shares are liquid, so large amounts of capital can be raised.

options.text: Every shareholder has equal authority to bind the company to contracts.
options.explanation: This describes a partnership-style agency relationship. A corporation is a separate legal entity and does not work this way.

mcqs.stem: Compared with a regular corporation, which description best fits a limited liability company (LLC)?

options.text: Owners are fully liable for debts, and profit is taxed at the entity level.
options.explanation: This reverses both features. An LLC gives liability protection and usually does not tax profit at the entity level.

options.text: Owners have limited liability, and profit typically passes through to their personal tax returns.
options.explanation: Correct. The LLC combines corporate-style liability protection with partnership-style pass-through taxation.

options.text: Owners are fully liable for debts, and profit passes through to personal returns.
options.explanation: This describes a general partnership. It misses the liability protection that defines an LLC.

mcqs.stem: Three founders want to share management, avoid a separate tax on the entity's profit, and make sure none of them can be forced to pay the others' business debts from personal assets. Which form fits best?

options.text: General partnership
options.explanation: It avoids entity-level tax, but each general partner has unlimited liability, including for the other partners' actions.

options.text: Regular C corporation
options.explanation: It gives limited liability, but profit is taxed at the corporate level and again on dividends, which fails the tax goal.

options.text: Limited liability company
options.explanation: Correct. Members get liability protection and the usual pass-through tax treatment, and voting follows ownership interests.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the drawbacks of a sole proprietorship is most accurate?

options.text: Its profit is taxed first at the business level and again when paid to the owner.
options.explanation: This is double taxation, which applies to regular corporations. Sole proprietors report business income only on their personal returns.

options.text: The owner must share control with co-owners, and the shareholders can freely sell their stakes.
options.explanation: A sole proprietor has no co-owners or shares. This describes a corporation, not a proprietorship.

options.text: Its life ends with the owner, and funding depends largely on the owner's own resources.
options.explanation: Correct. The business is tied to its owner, and unlimited liability plus a single owner make large outside financing difficult.

flashcards.front: What is double taxation, and which business form does it mainly affect?
flashcards.back: Profit is taxed at the corporate level, then taxed again on the shareholder's return when it is paid out as dividends. It mainly affects regular (C-type) corporations.

flashcards.front: How do a general partner and a limited partner differ in a limited partnership?
flashcards.back: The general partner runs the business and has unlimited liability. A limited partner is passive and can lose only the amount invested.

flashcards.front: What does a limited liability company (LLC) combine?
flashcards.back: Corporate-style limited liability for owners plus partnership-style pass-through taxation, which avoids double taxation.

flashcards.front: Why do sole proprietorships and general partnerships struggle to raise large amounts of capital?
flashcards.back: Owners face unlimited liability, the business is tied to its owners, and ownership interests are hard to transfer, so outside investors are reluctant.
